strengths: The paper asks a relevant question: whether optimization methods that improve generalization can also increase membership leakage. Examining SAM’s gains across individual-example groups provides a useful perspective beyond aggregate accuracy.

The experiments cover four image and tabular datasets, several attack families, additional model architectures, and five reported repetitions. The appendix provides substantial information about training hyperparameters and attack definitions.

SharpReg is straightforward to implement and substantially reduces the tested attacks. On CIFAR-100, single-query attack accuracy decreases from 76.68% for SGD to 59.64%, with task accuracy decreasing from 79.92% to 75.86%.
weaknesses: The central memorization explanation is not established. Section 3 groups examples using precomputed influence scores from SGD-trained models; it never directly measures whether SAM increases their memorization. Improved performance on these groups could reflect better representations or greater improvement opportunities on difficult examples. Optimizer-specific influence measurements, controls for baseline difficulty, and connections to individual-example membership leakage are needed.

The attack results contain a significant unresolved consistency issue. For balanced member/nonmember evaluation, the correctness attack in Eq. (8) has accuracy approximately (training accuracy + 1 - test accuracy)/2. Table 4’s CIFAR-100 SGD accuracies imply approximately 59.84%, whereas Table 3 reports 77.04%. The exact attack-set sizes and balancing are insufficiently specified. These numbers require reconciliation to establish confidence in the evaluation.

The influence-entropy metric needs stronger validation. Equation (3) is undefined when every influence is zero, yet Appendix C.1 assigns 2,153 such examples to the highest-entropy bucket by convention. Absence of measured influence does not establish broadly distributed influence. Sensitivity to this convention, estimation noise, and bucket thresholds is missing; the detailed analysis is also confined to CIFAR-100.

The privacy conclusions exceed the demonstrated scope. Although SAM increases the strongest reported attack accuracy, Table 1 shows lower multi-query accuracy on CIFAR-100 (69.18% to 65.41%) and CIFAR-10 (56.36% to 54.01%). The Purchase-100 single-query increase is only 0.29 percentage points, smaller than the reported standard deviations. These findings support a qualified result about particular attacks and settings, rather than a general relationship between flatness and privacy.

SharpReg’s proposed anti-overfitting mechanism is not isolated. For every reported xi < 1, Eq. (5) equals (1-xi) times Eq. (4), with lambda replaced by lambda/(1-xi). Although Appendix C.4.1 acknowledges parameter reduction, the interpretation of the added term as a distinct mechanism encouraging nonzero training loss remains unsupported. Comparisons must control effective sharpness weight, learning rate, and weight decay.

The defense comparisons do not convincingly establish a competitive accuracy–privacy tradeoff. Table 4’s SELENA result dominates the highlighted CIFAR-100 SharpReg configuration in task accuracy and both attack accuracies. Tuned conventional regularization and early-stopped SGD at matched utility are missing, and the claimed efficiency advantage lacks timing or compute measurements.

Privacy evaluation relies on aggregate attack accuracy without stronger example-calibrated attacks, such as likelihood-ratio attacks, or true-positive rates at low false-positive rates. This is especially limiting for claims concerning atypical, potentially vulnerable examples. The description of repetitions emphasizes attack-data splits and leaves variability across independently trained target models unclear.
